Introduction:
The potential outcomes framework is the dominant causal-inference framework in epidemiology [ 1–6 ]. Generally, under this framework, causal effects are defined as a contrast of outcomes that would happen among study participants if they were exposed (i.e. their potential outcomes if exposed) with outcomes that would happen among those same participants if they were unexposed (i.e. their potential outcomes if unexposed) [ 1 , 7–9 ]. Textbook guidance generally considers at least three assumptions key for estimating causal effects: (i) exchangeability, (ii) positivity, and (iii) consistency, our focus, which is that an individual’s outcome under the exposure they actually receive equals their potential outcome under that exposure [ 10 , 11 ]. Different, interrelated terms refer to the conditions under which consistency is met (e.g. the stable unit treatment value assumption) [ 12 , 13 ]. In epidemiology, the terms ‘well-defined intervention assumption’ [ 14 ] and ‘treatment variation irrelevance’ [ 15 ] are commonly used to describe ways consistency can be obtained.

Consistency is violated when there are multiple versions of the same exposure that have different effects on the outcome for the same individual [ 12 , 14 , 15 ]. Such exposures do not meet the well-defined intervention assumption [ 1 , 14 , 16 ]. Consider a randomized controlled trial (RCT) of an antidepressant in which participants are assigned to treatment arms clearly defined in all facets relevant to the outcome (e.g. dosage, duration, manufacturer); here, the well-defined intervention assumption would be satisfied. In contrast, consider an RCT in which there are different manufacturers who use varying formulations for what is labelled the same antidepressant, and the different formulations produce different treatment effects for some individuals. Here, some participants would have multiple potential outcomes for what is labelled a single treatment. Moreover, the estimated overall treatment effect in the study would be an average of the (potentially heterogeneous) effects of the different treatment versions in the sample [ 17 , 18 ]. Articulating a well-defined intervention would require specifying the manufacturer for each participant or including only one of the manufacturers. Alternatively, if there were no variation in the formulations’ effects, the well-defined intervention assumption would be satisfied because of treatment variation irrelevance, i.e. there may be treatment variation, but such variation is not relevant for the treatment’s effects on the outcome [ 15 ].

To satisfy the well-defined intervention assumption, textbooks and guidelines advocate conceptualizing exposures as treatments in hypothetical RCTs, even in observational settings [ 10 , 19 , 20 ]. Thus, when the well-defined intervention assumption is satisfied (along with other assumptions), causal effects can be interpreted as intervention effects: the effect an exposure would have on an outcome if it were modified by the hypothetical intervention [ 1 , 14 , 21 ]. This framing has several purported advantages. First, it encourages careful definition of exposures and causal contrasts, aiding satisfaction of consistency and estimation of precise causal effects [ 1 , 14 , 21 ]. Second, it enhances the potential for falsifying results of observational studies in actual RCTs, the ostensible gold standard for causal inference [ 1 , 22 ]. Third, it facilitates predicting the effects of actual interventions, making findings policy relevant [ 1 , 14 , 23 ]. For the latter two reasons, proponents encourage conceptualizing humanly feasible hypothetical interventions, although feasibility is not required [ 1 , 14 ].

According to textbooks and guidelines, specifying how an exposure would be intervened upon is key for estimating intervention effects, because different ‘hows’ can have different health effects [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 24 ]. Thus, failing to specify and operationalize the ‘how’ can cause consistency violations [ 1 , 14 , 22 ]. For example, consider a study aiming to estimate the effect on cognition of an intervention to increase physical activity by 2 h weekly over 10 years. In such a study, specifying how physical activity is increased would be key. Indeed, increasing it via boxing matches may have different effects on cognition than increasing it via running [ 25 , 26 ]. Alternatively, cogent arguments using theory, prior research or sensitivity analyses about why the ‘how’ would not matter for the intervention’s likely effects on the outcome (i.e. arguments for treatment variation irrelevance [ 15 ]) may suffice [ 16 , 27 ].

As the interventional framing and well-defined intervention assumption become more widely adopted, ‘causal effects’ and ‘intervention effects’ become synonyms [ 5 , 21–23 , 28 , 29 ]. Nonetheless, as with any new approach or framework, there may differences between what guidelines advise and what researchers do in practice [ 10 , 11 , 30–34 ]. Additionally, applying the interventional framework in epidemiology may present unique challenges, as epidemiological studies are frequently observational, analysing non-interventional exposures. Moreover, epidemiological datasets often lack sufficient detail from which to operationalize well-defined interventions (e.g. datasets may contain information on respondents’ duration of physical activity but lack information on activity type). In such settings, satisfying the well-defined intervention assumption can be challenging. Because of these challenges, best practices require transparent discussion of researchers’ reasoning regarding satisfaction of causal inference assumptions, including the well-defined intervention assumption [ 16 ].

In summary, although the well-defined intervention assumption has been widely accepted as key for estimating causal effects, satisfying the assumption can be problematic in common epidemiological settings. However, to our knowledge, no studies have systematically evaluated adherence to best practices regarding the assumption in epidemiological research. Thus, we investigated how epidemiologists using g-methods or targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) [ 10 , 35–37 ] interpreted and addressed the well-defined intervention assumption in their observational studies. Our overall objective was to assess whether researchers who aimed to estimate the effects of hypothetical interventions followed best practices regarding the well-defined intervention assumption [ 10 ]. Specifically, we examined: (i) whether authors articulated explicitly causal objectives; (ii) whether authors stated their exposure contrast of interest in terms of a hypothetical intervention; (iii) if so, whether authors specified well-defined interventions supported by their data; (iv) whether authors discussed key causal inference assumptions, particularly consistency; and (v) how authors interpreted their findings, particularly given their discussion of assumptions.
Methods:
### Article selection

We searched PubMed on 22 February 2021 for articles that: (i) were published from 2000–21 [ 38 ], (ii) were in the six general epidemiology journals with the highest 2020 impact factors [ 39 ], and (iii) included terms in their titles or abstracts related to g-methods or TMLE. Figure 1 displays our specific search criteria and terms.

We imported articles from PubMed into Covidence, a systematic-review data management tool [ 40 ]. Two reviewers (J.E.G. and K.L.K.) screened and included articles for data extraction if they: (i) were original research articles presenting findings from an observational study, (ii) used g-methods or TMLE, either as a primary aim or an emphasized secondary aim, and (iii) focused primarily on substantive research (not methodological development). We focused on studies using g-methods or TMLE because: (a) they often aim to estimate causal effects, for which the well-defined intervention assumption is relevant, and (b) g-methods and TMLE were developed using the potential outcomes framework as a foundation, making such studies particularly likely to consider the assumption. Figure 1 displays specific inclusion/exclusion criteria.

### Data extraction

The two reviewers independently extracted article data using a Google Forms tool. Reviewers focused on the primary study aim when extracting data, unless only a secondary aim used g-methods or TMLE, in which case reviewers focused on that aim. We organized the tool by manuscript section. If the answer to a question was unavailable in the designated section (e.g. Methods) but available in a different one (e.g. Results), reviewers answered the question using information from that section. Reviewers generally only used information explicitly provided by study authors to answer questions (i.e. they avoided inferring information on behalf of authors).

Reviewers extracted article metadata, including journal, publication year, title and subject area; each article could be assigned multiple subject areas.

From the Introduction, reviewers categorized the study’s objectives as: (i) ‘clearly causal’, when authors used explicitly causal language to describe the exposure-outcome relationship (e.g. ‘…the causal/interventional effect of…’), or (ii) ‘not clearly causal’, when authors used non-causal language (e.g. ‘…the association between…’) or a mix of causal and associational language [ 32 ].

From the Methods, reviewers first assessed whether authors stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention. Then, among studies in which this was the case (‘intervention-effect studies’), reviewers assessed if authors stated how the exposure would be intervened upon or changed. Among studies that provided a ‘how’, reviewers assessed if the stated intervention: (i) likely produced consistency, (ii) was practicably ‘actionable’ [ 1 ] or ‘feasible’ [ 1 ], (iii) could be implemented and tested in an RCT, and (iv) was supported by the data (i.e. the analytical variable matched the description of the hypothetical intervention [ 1 ]). Among studies in which authors did not provide a ‘how’, reviewers assessed if the ‘how’ mattered for the exposure’s or intervention’s likely effects on the outcome (i.e. if it mattered for consistency). As elsewhere, when assessing adherence to consistency, reviewers relied—when possible—on information regarding the assumption provided by authors; when authors did not provide such information, reviewers relied heavily on discussions in the epidemiological methods literature regarding consistency in studies of certain exposures [e.g. body mass index (BMI)] [ 1 , 14 , 16 ]. Reviewers also extracted the specific analytical method used.

From the Results/Discussion, reviewers first assessed if authors mentioned (i.e. at least listed as a condition for causal inference) the assumptions of consistency (or related terms), exchangeability and positivity. Next, reviewers assessed if authors discussed their findings in terms of intervention or policy relevance, and if authors stated predictions about what would happen to outcome burdens if their specific exposure contrast was applied in the real world. Subsequently, among intervention-effect studies, reviewers assessed if authors discussed intervention feasibility. Finally, among intervention-effect studies, reviewers assessed if authors explicitly interpreted their estimates as corresponding to the effects of a hypothetical intervention (versus a non-interventional causal effect, association, or otherwise).

Finally, considering all extracted data, reviewers assessed if intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions. Recognizing that no study is perfect, all causal effects are vague to some degree and we are not experts in all subfields, we concluded a study had a well-defined intervention if: (i) authors specified a ‘how’ that reasonably adhered to consistency, or (ii) when authors did not specify a ‘how’, they cogently argued for treatment variation irrelevance or, more generally, why consistency was likely satisfied or why consistency violations were likely inconsequential. In the absence of (i) or (ii), reviewers relied heavily on the epidemiological methods literature to inform their assessments.

### Conflicts

We resolved conflicts via discussions between the two primary reviewers, and when necessary, co-author consultation.

### Analysis

We tabulated the distribution of responses to each question, including separately for intervention-effect and non-intervention-effect studies. We did not calculate confidence intervals for our estimates because we did not aim to generalize beyond our sample. Our data and code are available at [ https://osf.io/knuc3/?view_only=bf24f8fb4f4947be86148e4b90d00e1a] , which contains the list of reviewed articles.
Results:
### Search and screening

Our PubMed search yielded 362 articles, 216 of which did not meet inclusion criteria, leaving 146 for review ( Figure 1 ).

### Data extraction

Supplementary Table S1 , available at IJE online, contains examples of extracted data and reviewers’ assessments.

Most included studies were published in American Journal of Epidemiology (67/146, 46%) or Epidemiology (35/146, 24%) ( Table 1 ). The median publication year was 2016. The most common subject areas were mortality (53/146, 36%) and social determinants (38/146, 26%).

We categorized 20% of studies (29/146, Table 2 ) as intervention-effect studies because they stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention ( Supplementary Table S2 , available at IJE online, contains details). Among them, 90% (26/29) had clearly causal objectives, compared with just 45% (53/117) of non-intervention-effect studies. Most intervention-effect studies used the parametric g-formula/g-computation alone to estimate their exposure contrast (22/29, 76%), whereas most non-intervention-effect studies used inverse probability weighting (IPW)/marginal structural modelling (MSM) alone (87/117, 74%).

Of the 29 intervention-effect studies, only one (3%) detailed how the exposure would be intervened upon ( Table 2 ). In this study, the ‘how’ adhered to consistency, as the hypothetical intervention compared the effects on child growth and mortality of narrowly defined antiretroviral treatment strategies. Moreover, the ‘how’ was ‘feasible’, could be implemented in an RCT and was supported by the data. The absence of a specified ‘how’ in other intervention-effect studies is notable because we concluded that in most (18/28, 64%), the ‘how’ mattered for consistency, i.e. for the exposure’s likely effects on the outcome.

Of the three causal-inference assumptions, studies mentioned exchangeability most frequently (134/146, 92%); a minority mentioned consistency (62/146, 42%) or positivity (66/146, 45%) ( Table 2 ). However, intervention-effect studies mentioned all assumptions more frequently [28/29 (97%) mentioned exchangeability, 23/29 (79%) mentioned consistency, and 15/29 (52%) mentioned positivity]. Just 34% (40/117) of non-intervention-effect studies discussed results’ intervention or policy relevance, compared with 59% (17/29) of intervention-effect studies. Only 41% (12/29) of intervention-effect studies discussed intervention feasibility, and few studies of either type (≤10%) stated predictions about what would happen to outcome burdens if their exposure contrast was applied in the real world. Finally, authors explicitly interpreted their estimates as corresponding to hypothetical intervention effects in 45% (13/29) of intervention-effect studies.

Only 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions ( Table 2 ; interrater reliability: kappa = 0.85). Of the 10 most common subject areas among intervention-effect studies, occupational studies and/or cancer studies most frequently had well-defined interventions ( Supplementary Table S3 , available at IJE online). Only one study had a well-defined intervention because it articulated an intervention ‘how’ that adhered to consistency ( Table 3 ). The other 10 had well-defined interventions—without articulating a ‘how’ — because of treatment variation irrelevance. In these studies, authors often described what their intervention was (e.g. reduce an exposure to a regulatory limit) and discussed why the mechanisms through which the intervention could be achieved (i.e. the ‘how’) would likely have similar effects on the outcome. In such cases, when possible, we deferred to the authors’ subject-area expertise in concluding the studies had well-defined interventions. For example, one study aimed to estimate the effect of a hypothetical intervention to reduce diesel-exhaust exposure on lung-cancer mortality among miners ( Table 3 ). According to the authors, reducing exposure through an intervention that improves ventilation would likely have similar effects on lung-cancer mortality as an intervention that reduces it via cleaner fuel or otherwise.

In contrast, no intervention-effect studies of obesity/BMI, substance use, health behaviours, nutrition and/or physical activity had well-defined interventions ( Supplementary Table S3 , available at IJE online). In these studies, authors often described what their intervention was, but did not discuss why the various mechanisms through which the intervention could be achieved (i.e. the ‘hows’) would likely have similar effects on the outcome. In such cases, when possible, we deferred to the methods literature in assessing the plausibility of treatment variation irrelevance and the well-defined intervention assumption. For example, one study aimed to estimate the effect of a hypothetical intervention to reduce BMI on all-cause mortality, but neither specified a ‘how’ nor cogently argued for treatment variation irrelevance ( Table 3 ). However, exercise-induced weight loss likely has different mortality effects compared with weight loss from medication, diet, illness or otherwise. Further, BMI (like many other exposures we classified as ill-defined) is a prototypical example of an exposure that often produces consistency violations [ 1 , 14 , 16 ]. Thus, when studies of such exposures simply stated—without justification—that treatment variation irrelevance was assumed (or ignored the assumption entirely), we concluded they had ill-defined interventions.
Discussion:
### Summary

Evaluating 146 articles in top epidemiology journals, we investigated how researchers using g-methods or TMLE interpreted and addressed the well-defined intervention assumption in their observational studies.

Most studies had clearly causal objectives. However, despite the interventional framework’s growing prominence, only 20% (29/146) of studies stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention. Of these intervention-effect studies, only 3% (1/29) detailed ‘how’ the exposure would be intervened upon. Of those that did not provide a ‘how’, we concluded the ‘how’ mattered for consistency (i.e. treatment variation irrelevance likely did not hold) in 64% (18/28) of studies. Thus, we concluded just 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions.

We also observed concerning findings regarding studies’ adherence to best practices for causal inference more broadly. For example, although intervention-effect studies most often mentioned causal-inference assumptions, 21% (6/29) did not mention consistency and 48% (14/29) did not mention positivity. Notably across studies, consistency, exchangeability and positivity were often not robustly discussed, but rather simply listed as requirements for causal inference. For example, some intervention-effect studies (including those that lacked a well-defined intervention) stated consistency was required for estimating causal effects, but: (i) did not discuss the likelihood the assumption held, or (ii) acknowledged probable consistency violations without discussing how they might affect findings. This defies best practices of being transparent about a study’s assumptions and arguing for their satisfaction (or explaining the implications of violations for inference) [ 16 ].

### Explanation of findings

One explanation for non-adherence to best practices for addressing the well-defined intervention assumption, even when using methods designed to enhance causal inference, is the lag between the development of new approaches and their appropriate use in applied research. Indeed, recent reviews have observed nonadherence to best practices in the use of directed acyclic graphs [ 33 ], alignment between study goals and the variable selection methods used to address them [ 32 , 41 ], reporting of interaction [ 42 ], and assessment of mediation-analysis assumptions [ 43 ], among other areas [ 44 ].

Our findings may also reflect the well-defined intervention assumption’s contested status. For example, critics have argued the assumption restricts the field’s purview to narrowly defined exposures that can be conceptualized as treatments in hypothetical RCTs, marginalizing research on exposures not directly manipulable by biomedical or public-health interventions, including research on socio-structural factors [ 2 , 45–47 ]. In response, some proponents have downplayed the importance of intervention feasibility [ 48 ] and even implied that articulating the ‘how’ is unnecessary as long as there is ‘consensus’ that the ‘how’ would not matter for consistency [ 49 , 50 ].

In this context, applied epidemiologists may have recognized the difficulty of adhering to the assumption but lack knowledge of alternative causal-inference frameworks. Our findings suggest they have largely continued researching the causal effects of socio-structural factors and other challenging exposures (e.g. BMI), while circumventing or overlooking the specifics of the well-defined intervention assumption. In our review, this typically manifested in two approaches. In the more common approach, particularly for those with socio-structural exposures, studies avoided using the interventional framework altogether but did not explicitly adopt alternatives, even though non-interventional causal interpretations have been proposed for such exposures [ 51 , 52 ]. As evidence, whereas ‘social determinants’ was the second most common subject area of reviewed studies overall, it was rare among intervention-effect studies (12th most common of 22, eAppendix 2 available at IJE online). Instead, authors often stated their aims were to estimate ‘associations’ or ambiguous ‘effects’, yet occasionally still evaluated the validity of the well-defined intervention assumption (or related assumptions) in Discussion sections, implying intervention effects were of interest, despite signalling otherwise. That almost no study explicitly aimed to estimate non-interventional causal effects, like aetiological effects or realized effects [ 51–55 ], suggests the need for exposure to alternative non-interventional causal-inference frameworks in epidemiological training. In the less common approach, studies aimed to estimate intervention effects but failed to either: (i) articulate a ‘how’, let alone one that was well-defined, or (ii) cogently argue for treatment variation irrelevance. Thus, whereas using the interventional framework may help researchers explicitly state their objectives, articulate their estimands and acknowledge the assumptions underpinning findings’ validity, researchers’ engagement with the framework’s specifics—particularly the assumptions—is often rote and uncritical.

### Recommendations

Minimally, researchers aiming to estimate intervention effects should specify a ‘how’ that adheres to consistency and is supported by their data (or at least cogently argue for treatment variation irrelevance) [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 24 ]. Indeed, carefully specifying a ‘how’ is often key for adhering to consistency and anticipating the effects of hypothetical interventions [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 24 ]. Moreover, a core argument for articulating well-defined interventions is that specifying a ‘how’, particularly a feasible ‘how’, makes findings policy-relevant [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 23 ]. Following guidelines, like those outlined in the target-trial framework, may facilitate this process [ 31 ]. Conversely, researchers aiming to estimate alternative causal effects should be explicit about their estimand of interest and the assumptions required for causal inference, which may not include the well-defined intervention assumption [ 17 , 31 ]. For example, in a study in which the assumption is violated—but exchangeability and positivity hold—the estimated overall exposure effect will correspond to the effect the exposure actually had in the sample, averaged across the different ways that participants came to be exposed [ 17 , 18 ]. This realized causal effect may be an internally valid estimate of the exposure effect in the sample, but does not correspond to an intervention effect and will not predict what the effect of an intervention on the exposure would be [ 17 ]. This effect is often of interest, e.g. when aiming to identify the causes of population patterns of disease over a given period [ 51–53 ]. Thus, non-interventional causal-inference frameworks may merit more frequent use, particularly given the challenges of adhering to the well-defined intervention assumption. Finally, researchers aiming to estimate associations should be similarly explicit about their aims and assumptions [ 16 , 32 , 56 ]. Our recommendations align with recent studies highlighting the need for improved clarity of objectives and application of causal-inference approaches in epidemiology [ 32 , 33 , 56 ].

### Limitations

In our review, we generally only extracted information explicitly provided by authors to limit the influence of reviewer subjectivity, and two reviewers extracted all information, arriving at consensus. However, our assessments of whether studies had well-defined interventions were subjective and sometimes required subject-area expertise, and we are not experts in all subfields. Nonetheless, when possible, we relied on information provided by authors regarding satisfaction of consistency, although such information was often not provided. Without such information, we relied heavily on the methods literature to inform our assessments. An additional limitation is that some extracted data may have been influenced by journal requirements (e.g. Epidemiology discourages discussing results’ policy relevance [ 57 ]) and thus not reflect researchers’ predilections alone.
Conclusion: We found substantial deviations between guidelines regarding meeting the well-defined intervention assumption and researchers’ application of the guidelines, with intervention-effect studies rarely having well-defined interventions. We call for more careful treatment of the assumption in epidemiological research.
Ethics approval: This study was exempt from IRB review and informed consent requirements.
